title: Sticking to the melody, limited range and mouthpiece
summary: He explains his melodic style, small range, high notes and a medium mouthpiece, and his poor early foundation on trumpet.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: I noticed when you play, you never played as wild as some of the trumpet players do. A lot of high notes and runs all over the place. I mean, was that sort of part of your style to stick to the melody more?
Yeah, yeah. That was most of life. Do stick close to the melody.
I think it sounds better that way than let the clarinet take the variations as they say. But I was wondering if that was part of your system and style that you tried to do that way.
Yeah, yeah. That was pretty much my style thing. Just stick close to the melody.
I like the trumpet myself and the clarinet down in that lower range, not screaming high. Of course Armstrong plays nice up high too.
Yes, yes. Well, I could never play very high on trumpet anyhow. My range was, you know, a small range. My range wasn't too wide.
Do you think that runs people's lips to go up too high sometime?
Well, sometimes it does because, you know, if you don't lift those things right, don't play them right while you bust a little piece of trying to.
What kind of a mouthpiece do you use or did you use in those days?
No, I just used a regular, regular, ordinary mouthpiece. I could never use a made-up mouthpiece. I think, what was it, a con-mouthpiece or a hold-on? I think I had a hold-on mouthpiece.
Wasn't extra deep or extra shallow or anything, just medium?

No, just a medium. Just a medium. Just an ordinary medium. Yeah. But I never played, never had a wide range on trumpet. Well, in fact, I just, I didn't really, didn't get started properly on trumpet, you know. Anyhow, and that makes a big difference in playing those.
